title: The London System
standfirst: Every opening so far has been a conversation — you play, they reply, the line branches. The London barely branches at all, which is exactly why it has taken over club chess.

steps.title: A system, not a line
body: Most openings are dialogues: each of your moves depends on their last one. A system is different — you aim for the same setup almost regardless of what your opponent does.
That means far less to remember. The trade-off is that you're not trying to punish anything specific; you're just getting a good position, every time.

steps.title: A standard reply
body: Black plays the most natural move. The London would look much the same against 1…Nf6 or 1…e6.

steps.title: Part of the setup
body: Knight to f3 is one of the five London moves. It happens nearly every game.

steps.title: Out before the pawn — this is the London
body: The move the system is named for. Compare the Queen's Gambit Declined, where White plays e3 and only then tries to solve the c1 bishop.
The bishop leaves the house before the door is shut. It's the same principle the Caro-Kann and Slav use for Black — get the bishop out before your own pawn traps it.

steps.title: Solid and standard
body: Black shuts in his own light-squared bishop, which the London player is quite happy to see.

steps.title: Now the pawn, safely
body: Supporting d4 and opening the f1 bishop. This move would have been careless three moves ago; it's perfectly fine now that the dark-squared bishop is outside.

steps.title: The standard lever
body: Black hits the base of White's little centre — the same idea as …c5 in the French. Good players play this against the London almost automatically.

steps.title: Hold everything together
body: A modest pawn that props up d4 and completes the London's pawn triangle: d4, e3, c3. Solid, unambitious, and very hard to break down.

steps.title: Pressure the centre
body: Black adds another attacker to d4.

steps.title: The last piece takes its square
body: Not c3, which is occupied by White's own pawn — the knight goes behind the pawns instead, heading for e5 or c4 later.

steps.title: The complete London setup
body: There is the system: pawns on c3, d4 and e3, knights on f3 and d2, bishop on f4, and the king about to castle. You will reach this position again and again.
Black challenges the London bishop, which usually retreats to g3. White's plan is Ne5, supported by the knight on d2, followed by a kingside build-up. Learn one plan, play it forever.
